A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HACO, with readable main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices. Corresponding material can be matched despite reference relocation, appendix expansion and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original dense hand contact experiments, component and backbone ablations, and downstream grasp optimization and reconstruction results in Tables 2–7 and A1–A3.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments, including revised existing results, additional baseline comparisons and a training-dataset-size ablation in Tables A2–A5.

M1.justification: Relative to v1's direct VCB supervision, Section 3.3 of v2 specifies a progressive CB-to-VCB weighting schedule and an additional false-positive regularizer. These extend the stated training procedure while retaining the architecture, balanced contact sampling and core VCB formulation. The PDFs do not establish when these additions entered the implementation.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 14 datasets and cover the same hand interaction types, dense contact estimation and two downstream tasks. The new comparisons and reduced-data ablation reuse existing datasets; HIC, RICH and Hi4D were already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: V2 adds MANO-based, retrained hand variants of POSA, BSTRO and DECO in Table A3. Table A4 adds direct contact comparisons with DefConNet, CHOI Stage 1, DICE InteractionNet, LatentAct's Data Engine and EasyHOI; EasyHOI previously appeared only in the downstream reconstruction comparison. Table A1 also removes the ObMan-mean initialization comparator.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 revises the reported training total from 840K to 655K images without explaining the difference. New experiments train hand-adapted baselines on the same 14 datasets, reproduce contact modules under specified configurations, and compare training on 1, 3 and 14 datasets. The resource table also replaces model memory with test memory. These are reported protocol changes and additions, not proof that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds a focused training-size ablation using MOW alone, three hand-object datasets and all 14 datasets (A.7, Table A5). It also removes the ObMan-mean condition from the initialization ablation. Existing sampling, loss, interaction-composition and backbone analyses remain, although their reported scores are revised.

E5.justification: V1 provides no seed or repeated-run information. V2's checklist newly states that results came from randomly seeded runs without cherry-picking and explicitly acknowledges absent error bars. It supplies no run counts, seed values, confidence intervals or significance tests, so increased repetition is not established.

E6.justification: Many results are revised: HACO's MOW F1 changes from 0.531 to 0.522, while Table 4 changes full-model RICH F1 from 0.528 to 0.781 and Hi4D F1 from 0.828 to 0.565. Backbone scores and rankings also change. V2 adds extensive baseline results in Tables A2–A4 and training-size results in A5. Given the revised training total and procedure description, these are not established same-setting gains or losses. Downstream Tables 6–7 remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds self-connections to the adjacency specification and maximum normalization of neighborhood contact and non-contact aggregates before the isolation score. This alters the described mathematical construction of the smoothness loss, although the displayed Equations (1)–(14) remain unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: V1 describes very few prior attempts at learning from diverse hand contacts. V2 strengthens this to no prior attempt and explicitly claims HACO is the first dense hand contact method trained on a large-scale dataset. The central BCS/VCB contributions and claims of contact-estimation and downstream benefits remain.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's self-contact limitation, v2 discusses missing temporal context, possible failure of mean-based BCS on multimodal distributions, weak hand-hand performance and the inability of positive-hand-only evaluation to assess hand-level false positives. Appendix A.6 also interprets the new controlled comparisons as evidence for task-specific design beyond training-data scale. These substantially expand the paper's qualifications and interpretation.

D1.justification: V2 reports publicly available code and provides a repository address, replacing v1's release promise. It adds smoothness-loss implementation details and explains baseline reproduction, replacement of body-model components with MANO, HaMeR mesh inputs, and use of reproduced versus released implementations. Test-memory measurements replace model-memory figures. These materially expand access and reproduction information, although some new loss parameters remain unspecified.

R1.justification: Appendix A.6 substantially broadens positioning from full-body contact estimators to learned and heuristic hand-contact modules, explaining their earlier exclusion and distinguishing HACO's standalone role. Ten cited works are added, including DICE, LatentAct and SAM2. Previously cited CHOI remains and gains direct evaluation; its disappearance from the main related-work paragraph is not removal from the paper.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact, with localized rewriting and clearer distinctions between vertices and hand instances. V2 adds acknowledgements and a NeurIPS checklist, moves references before the appendix, and inserts two appendix subsections. Most existing exposition is retained rather than extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: V2 adds four substantive appendix tables, A2–A5, and a ground-truth column to Figure 3. The previous backbone and resource tables become A6 and A7; the initialization table loses one row and the resource table changes its memory column. Existing qualitative predictions and appendix figures are retained. The expansion of comparison displays is substantial beyond pagination changes.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses a central weakness of v1's evidence: Table A3 compares against hand-adapted baselines trained on the same 14 datasets, reducing confounding from training coverage and body representation, while Table A4 adds relevant hand-contact competitors. Explicit evaluation limitations and reported code access further improve transparency. Unexplained revisions to sample totals and scores, incomplete new loss specifications and absent uncertainty estimates remain weaknesses, but the stronger comparative evidence provides a substantial net improvement.
